questions.correct_answer: Uniform convergence implies that the sequence of functions is Cauchy at each point x in the domain. Specifically, for a uniformly convergent sequence \((f_n)\) to f, for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists an N such that for all n \(\geq\) N and for all x \(\in\) E, \(|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon\). This means that for a fixed x, the sequence of numbers \((f_n(x))\) is a Cauchy sequence.
questions.explanation: Uniform convergence ensures that the convergence is not only fast but also 'uniform' across the entire domain. This uniformity implies that for any given \(\epsilon\), we can find a single N that works for all x. If we fix an x, then \(|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon\) for all n \(\geq\) N. This is precisely the definition of the sequence of numbers \((f_n(x))\) being a Cauchy sequence for that fixed x.
options: A Cauchy sequence is a sequence of functions that converges uniformly to a limit function. A sequence of functions converges uniformly if for every \(\\epsilon > 0\), there exists an N such that for all n, m > N, the absolute difference between the terms is less than \(\epsilon\).

A sequence of functions \((f_n)\) converges uniformly to a function f on a set E if for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that if \(d(x, y) < \delta\), then \(|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon\) for all n. A sequence \((x_n)\) is Cauchy if for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists an N such that for all n, m > N, \(|x_n - x_m| < \epsilon\).

A sequence of functions \((f_n)\) converges uniformly to a function f on a set E if for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists an integer N such that for all n \(\geq\) N and for all x \(\in\) E, \(|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon\). A sequence \((x_n)\) is Cauchy if for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists an N such that for all n, m > N, \(|x_n - x_m| < \epsilon\).

questions.correct_answer: The sequence \((f_n)\) converges pointwise to f(x) = 0 on [0, 1], but it does not converge uniformly. However, for each x, the sequence of numbers \((f_n(x))\) is a Cauchy sequence.
questions.explanation: For any fixed x \(\in\) [0, 1], \(f_n(x) = \frac{x}{n}\). As n \(\to\) \(\infty\), \(f_n(x) \to 0\). Thus, the sequence converges pointwise to f(x) = 0. To check for uniform convergence, we examine \(\sup_{x \in [0, 1]} |f_n(x) - f(x)| = \sup_{x \in [0, 1]} |\frac{x}{n} - 0| = \frac{1}{n}\). As n \(\to\) \(\infty\), \(\frac{1}{n} \to 0\), which means the convergence is uniform. For any fixed x, the sequence \((f_n(x)) = (\frac{x}{n})\) is a sequence of real numbers. Since it converges to 0, it is a Cauchy sequence.
options: The sequence \((f_n)\) converges uniformly to f(x) = 0 on [0, 1], and for each x, the sequence of numbers \((f_n(x))\) is a Cauchy sequence.
The sequence \((f_n)\) converges pointwise to f(x) = 0 on [0, 1], but it does not converge uniformly. However, for each x, the sequence of numbers \((f_n(x))\) is a Cauchy sequence.
The sequence \((f_n)\) converges uniformly to f(x) = 0 on [0, 1], but the sequence of numbers \((f_n(x))\) is not always a Cauchy sequence for each x.
